title: US Citizenship Civics Test: 2008 vs 2025 Version Explained
description: Which civics test you take depends on your N-400 filing date. See how the 2008 and 2025 versions differ in questions, passing score, and the 65/20 rule.
intro: USCIS now uses two versions of the naturalization civics test. The newer 2025 version has a longer question list, asks more questions at the interview, and needs more correct answers. The older 2008 version is still given to some people. Which one you take does not depend on your interview date. It depends on the day your Form N-400 was filed. This guide explains the dividing line, what changed in the numbers, what stayed the same, and what to study for your version.

sections.heading: The dividing line: your N-400 filing date
sections.body:
USCIS picks your test version by the date your naturalization application (Form N-400) was filed:

- **Filed before October 20, 2025**: you take the **2008** civics test.
- **Filed on or after October 20, 2025**: you take the **2025** civics test.

This matters most for people who filed in the months around that date. Your interview may be in 2026, but if your application was filed before October 20, 2025, the officer will use the 2008 test. So before you start studying, find the filing date of your N-400 in your USCIS records. Studying the wrong list wastes time, because the two lists are not the same length and many questions are worded differently.

sections.heading: What changed in the numbers
sections.body:
The USCIS Policy Manual describes both versions side by side:

- **Question list**: 100 questions (2008) became **128 questions** (2025).
- **Questions asked at the interview**: up to 10 (2008) became **up to 20** (2025).
- **Correct answers needed**: 6 (2008) became **12** (2025).
- **When the officer stops**: in 2008, after 6 correct or 5 wrong answers. In 2025, after **12 correct or 9 wrong** answers.

In plain terms, on the 2025 test you can miss up to 8 questions and still pass, as long as you reach 12 correct before you reach 9 wrong. On the 2008 test you could miss up to 4. The test is still oral: the officer reads the question and you answer out loud. There are no answer choices to pick from.

sections.heading: What stayed the same
sections.body:
Some important rules did not change:

- **The passing rate is still 60 percent.** 6 of 10 and 12 of 20 are both 60 percent.
- **Questions are picked at random** from the list. You cannot know in advance which ones you will get, so you need to know the whole list for your version.
- **Other wording can count.** The Policy Manual says an answer passes if it is correct or is a different way of saying the correct answer. Still, the official list itself encourages you to use the answers it gives, so learning those answers is the safest plan.
- **Two chances.** If you fail the civics or English part at your first interview, USCIS schedules a second try between 60 and 90 days later. The officer retests only the part you failed. Failing the same part a second time leads to denial of the application.

sections.heading: The 65/20 special consideration on each version
sections.body:
If you were **65 or older** and had lived in the United States as a lawful permanent resident for **20 years or more**, you may qualify for a shorter test. The Policy Manual says both conditions must be met at the time you file.

Under this rule you study only **20 specially marked questions**. On the 2025 list (USCIS form M-1778), these are the questions with an asterisk at the end. The officer asks **10 of them**, and you need **6 correct**. You may take the civics test in the language of your choice, with an interpreter.

The filing date rule still applies. If you qualify for 65/20, the version of that 20-question set you study is the one that matches your test version. Use the 2008 materials if you filed before October 20, 2025, and the 2025 materials if you filed on or after it.

sections.heading: Answers that change with elections
sections.body:
Some answers can change because of elections or appointments. Most of these questions ask for the name of a person who holds office now, such as the President or your state's Governor. USCIS says you must answer with the name of the official **serving at the time of your interview**, not the name printed in an older study guide.

USCIS lists these questions by number on its test updates page:

- **2025 version**: questions 23 (one of your state's U.S. Senators), 29 (your U.S. Representative), 30 (Speaker of the House), 38 (President), 39 (Vice President), 57 (Chief Justice), and 61 (your Governor).
- **2008 version**: questions 20, 23, 28, 29, 39, 40, 43, 46, and 47.

Three of the 2025 questions depend on where you live (your Senators, Representative, and Governor). This practice site leaves the changing and state-based questions out of its quizzes so that it never shows an out-of-date answer. Look these up on the USCIS test updates page in the week before your interview.

sections.heading: How the 128 questions are grouped on the 2025 list
sections.body:
The 2025 list has three parts. Using the official question numbers, this site splits it into nine chapters:

1. **American Government (questions 1 to 72)**: principles of government (1 to 15), Congress (16 to 35), the President and executive branch (36 to 49), courts and federal and state powers (50 to 62), and rights and responsibilities (63 to 72).
2. **American History (questions 73 to 118)**: colonial period and independence (73 to 89), the 1800s (90 to 99), and recent history (100 to 118).
3. **Symbols and Holidays (questions 119 to 128)**.

The largest chapters are Congress (20 questions) and recent history (19 questions). Government alone is 72 of the 128 questions, so it is the best place to start if you are short on time.

sections.heading: What to do this week
sections.body:
1. Find your N-400 filing date and decide which version you take: before October 20, 2025 means 2008; on or after means 2025.
2. Download the matching list from USCIS. For the 2025 version, that is **128 Civics Questions and Answers (M-1778)**. USCIS also offers the reader **One Nation, One People (2025 Version)**.
3. If you qualify for 65/20, mark the 20 special questions and study only those.
4. For the 2025 version, work through one chapter a day. As an example plan, the nine chapters above take nine days to cover once. Then repeat the larger chapters (Congress, recent history, principles).
5. Say each answer out loud. The real test is spoken, so practice speaking, not just reading.
6. In the week before your interview, check the USCIS test updates page for the current President, Vice President, Speaker, Chief Justice, and your own Senators, Representative, and Governor.

faq.question: I filed my N-400 in September 2025. Which test do I take?
faq.answer: The 2008 civics test. USCIS gives the 2008 version to everyone who filed before October 20, 2025, even if the interview takes place later.

faq.question: Is the 2025 civics test harder than the 2008 test?
faq.answer: The passing rate is the same, 60 percent, but there is more to learn. The list grew from 100 to 128 questions, and the officer can ask up to 20 questions instead of 10. You need 12 correct answers instead of 6.

faq.question: Can I say an answer in my own words?
faq.answer: The USCIS Policy Manual says a correct answer or another way of saying the correct answer is accepted. The official list encourages applicants to use the answers it provides, so learn those first.
